plan.text: Here is your plan for CSC2103 Data Structures final revision sprint. Your exam is on Wednesday 14 October at 9:00. You have 3 study days and 45 minutes a day. Last year's paper put 25 percent of the marks on Binary heaps: priority queue operations and 21 percent of the marks on Hash tables: the map ADT and hash functions. So you will learn 3 lessons: Hash tables: the map ADT and hash functions, Binary search trees: search, insert and delete and Binary heaps: priority queue operations. We cut Counting operations to get Big-O from real code, Big-O, Omega and Theta: which bound? and Dynamic arrays vs linked lists: layout and cost. Your reviews are dated backwards from the exam, so the last one lands the day before. Every answer was checked against your own files.

clips.text:
Binary search trees: search, insert and delete.
A BST is a binary tree with one extra rule: for every node, everything in its left subtree is smaller and everything in its right subtree is bigger. That single rule is what lets you search in O of h instead of scanning every node. Slide 3 of Lecture 3 fixes the vocabulary you will be marked on:
Slide 5 gives the search loop. It is iterative, not recursive: Each comparison sends you exactly one level down, so the cost is O of h. Insert is the same walk with one extra move: search for the key, and when the walk falls off the tree, attach a new leaf there.
Delete is the hard one, and it has three cases — slide 7 lists them. A leaf just goes. A node with one child is replaced by that child. A node with two children is replaced by its in-order successor, the smallest key in its right subtree, and then that successor is deleted from where it sat.
Why the successor and not just any node? Because in-order traversal of a BST visits keys in sorted order. Slide 6 shows it on the example tree: in-order gives 20 30 40 50 60 70 80, pre-order gives 50 30 20 40 70 60 80, post-order gives 20 40 30 60 80 70 50.
The successor is the next key in that sorted list, so putting it where the deleted node was keeps the sorted order intact.
Insert 40, 20, 60, 10, 30, 50, 70, 25 into an empty BST, then delete 20. Follow the comparisons — every insertion is one search that fails, plus one attach. Insert 40 — the root. The tree is empty, so 40 becomes the root. No comparisons needed. Insert 20 — go left. Start at 40. 20 40, so move to the left child.
It is null, so attach 20 there. Insert 60 — go right. Start at 40. 60 40, so move to the right child. It is null, so attach 60 there. Insert 10 — two lefts. 10 40 to left to 20. 10 20 to left of 20. Null, so attach. Insert 30 — left then right. 30 40 to left to 20. 30 20 to right of 20. Null, so attach.
Insert 50 and 70. 50 40 to right to 60. 50 60 to left of 60. Attach. Then 70 40 to right to 60. 70 60 to right of 60. Attach. Insert 25 — three comparisons. 25 40 to left to 20. 25 20 to right to 30. 25 30 to left of 30. Null, so attach. Delete 20 — two children, use the in-order successor.
20 has two children (10 and 30), so slide 7 says copy in the in-order successor. The successor is the smallest key in the right subtree of 20: walk right to 30, then left as far as possible. 30 has a left child, 25, and 25 has no left child, so the successor is 25.
Copy 25 into 20's slot, then delete the old 25 node, which is a leaf.
Slide 6's example tree has 50 at the root, with left subtree 30 (20, 40) and right subtree 70 (60, 80). Its in-order traversal is 20 30 40 50 60 70 80. Delete 50. It has two children, so slide 7 says use the in-order successor. Walk right from 50 to 70. Walk left as far as possible: 70 to 60 to 60 has no left child.
Successor is 60. Copy 60 into 50's slot. The root is now 60. Delete the old 60 node. It was the left child of 70 and had no children, so it just goes. Final tree: root 60, left child 30 (with 20 and 40), right child 70 (with 80 as its right child, no left child). In-order traversal: 20 30 40 60 70 80.
Sorted, and 50 is gone. Slide 7 states the same result: deleting 50 puts 60 at the root.
To delete a node with two children I can just promote either child into its place. Slide 7 gives the two-child rule as copying in the in-order successor, the smallest key in the right subtree, and then deleting that successor.
Promoting a child does not work in general: in the walkthrough tree, promoting 30 into 20's place would leave 30 needing two left children, 10 and its own left child 25, and a node has only one left link, so a subtree gets lost.
Copying the successor (25) changes one key and removes one leaf; every other link stays where it was. The difference is observable: run in-order traversal after the delete and a lost subtree shows up as missing keys.
You are tracing an exam question. The tree currently holds 40 at the root, with 20 (children 10 and 30) on the left and 60 (children 50 and 70) on the right. The question asks you to delete 40 and draw the result. You have one minute per decision.

Binary heaps: priority queue operations.
Slide 3 of Lecture 4 lists what a priority queue must do: every element carries a priority, and the highest-priority element leaves first. The operations are insert, peek (find-min or find-max), and extract-min or extract-max.
The applications on that slide are CPU and job scheduling, Dijkstra's shortest paths and Prim's minimum spanning tree, event-driven simulation, heapsort, and finding the k largest items in a stream. A binary heap is the structure that makes those operations cheap.
Slide 4 gives the two properties that define it, and both must hold at once: Shape property — a complete binary tree: every level is full except possibly the last, and the last fills from the left. Heap property — in a min-heap every parent is at most its children, so the minimum sits at the root.
(A max-heap reverses the comparison.) A heap is not sorted. Siblings have no order between them. In the array [1, 3, 6, 5, 9, 8], the children of the root are 3 and 6, and 5, 9, 8 sit under them in an order that carries no meaning. The shape property is what lets you drop pointers entirely.
Slide 5 stores the nodes level by level in an array with index 0 as the root, and for the node at index i: That array [1, 3, 6, 5, 9, 8] is the tree. Check it against the formulas. Index 1 holds 3; its children are indices 3 and 4, holding 5 and 9.
Index 2 holds 6; its left child is index 5, holding 8, and its right child would be index 6, which does not exist. Index 5's parent is Math.floor((5 - 1) / 2) = 2, holding 6. Every parent is at most its children, and the tree is complete, so this is a valid min-heap.
Because the shape is fixed, only two operations can ever disturb the heap, and each has exactly one repair: insert adds at the end and sifts up; extract-min moves the last leaf to the root and sifts down.
Slide 12 prices them: find-min is O of 1, insert and extract-min are O of log n, and building a heap from n items is O of n.
Slide 7 of Lecture 4 traces one insert into the heap [1, 3, 6, 5, 9, 8]. Here is the same procedure run on a different heap, with every array written out. Keep the array on paper and move the index with your finger — the exam marks the array after each swap, not just the final one.
Write the starting heap and confirm it is valid. Start from [4, 7, 9, 12, 8, 10]. Check the shape: indices 0 minus 5 exist, so the tree has a root, two children, and three leaves at indices 3, 4, 5 — level 0 full, level 1 full, level 2 filling from the left.
Check the heap property: index 1 holds 7 with children at 3 (12) and 4 (8), and 7 at most 12 and 7 at most 8. Index 2 holds 9 with left child at 5 (10), and 9 at most 10. Valid min-heap. Append the new key at the end. Insert 5. The new key goes at index 6 — the next free slot, which keeps the tree complete.
Array becomes [4, 7, 9, 12, 8, 10, 5]. Do not compare-and-place it anywhere else; the shape property forces the position. Find the parent of the new key. i = 6, so p = Math.floor((6 - 1) / 2) = Math.floor(2.5) = 2. Index 2 holds 9. Compare: is heap[2] = heap[6]?
9 at most 5 is false, so the heap property is violated and you must swap. Swap with the parent and move up. Swap indices 2 and 6: [4, 7, 5, 12, 8, 10, 9]. The 5 is now at index 2. Set i = 2 and repeat. Repeat at the new index. i = 2, so p = Math.floor((2 - 1) / 2) = 0. Index 0 holds 4. Compare: 4 at most 5 is true.
The heap property holds, so break out of the loop. No swap. Write the final array and verify. Final array: [4, 7, 5, 12, 8, 10, 9]. Verify every parent: index 0 (4) at most 7 and 5; index 1 (7) at most 12 and 8; index 2 (5) at most 10 and 9. Shape is still complete.
One swap, one level: sift-up makes at most one swap per level, so the cost is bounded by the height, O of log n.
Take the heap [4, 7, 5, 12, 8, 10, 9] from the walkthrough and run extractMin on it, following slide 8. Record the minimum. min = heap[0] = 4. This is what the function returns; it is not part of the array any more. Remove the last leaf. last = heap.pop() removes 9, leaving [4, 7, 5, 12, 8, 10].
The array is one shorter. Move the last leaf to the root. heap[0] = 9, giving [9, 7, 5, 12, 8, 10]. The shape is complete again, but the root is 9 and its children are 7 and 5 — the heap property is broken. Sift down from i = 0.
At i = 2 the left child is 10 and 9 10, so the node is already the smallest of the three and the loop breaks. Result. extractMin returns 4, and the heap is [5, 7, 9, 12, 8, 10]. Verify it: index 0 (5) at most 7 and 9; index 1 (7) at most 12 and 8; index 2 (9) at most 10.
One swap, one level down — the cost is the height, O of log n. Note what did not happen: the 9 did not travel to the bottom of the tree, and the array did not come back sorted. A heap only promises the root is the minimum.
The array [1, 3, 6, 5, 9, 8] is a heap, so it must be sorted — reading it left to right should give 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 9. Slide 4 states plainly that a heap is not sorted and that siblings have no order between them. The heap property constrains only parent-child pairs, never left-right pairs.
In [1, 3, 6, 5, 9, 8] the children of 3 are 5 and 9, and nothing requires 5 to come first — [1, 3, 6, 9, 5, 8] is an equally valid heap with the same keys.
The difference predicts real behaviour: find-min is O of 1 because the minimum is pinned at index 0, but finding the second-smallest key requires scanning the children of the root, and printing the heap in order requires heapsort — the O of n log n procedure on slide 11 — not a single pass.
Take the heap [2, 8, 5, 12, 9, 6]. Without running anything, predict the array after inserting 1, then after one extract-min on the original heap. Write both predictions down before you check them — which of the two traces did you get wrong, and which step in it slipped?

Hash tables: the map ADT and hash functions.
Slide 3 of Lecture 2 lists the dictionary (map) ADT as three operations: insert(key, value), search(key), delete(key). That is the whole contract. A map is not a list with nicer syntax — it is a promise that given a key you can get its value back, and the only question that matters on the exam is what each implementation charges you for that promise.
Slide 3 gives the price list: Read the table as a trade, not a ranking. An unsorted array inserts in O of 1 because you drop the pair at the end and walk away; search is O of n because nothing about the position tells you where the key is.
A sorted array buys O of log n search with binary search and pays O of n on insert, because a new key in the middle shifts everything after it. The balanced BST is the only one that refuses to be bad at either — O of log n both ways — and that is why it costs you pointer bookkeeping and rotations.
The hash table is the odd one out because it is the only row with the word average. Nothing about a hash table makes search O of 1 by construction. It makes search O of 1 when the keys are spread, and the rest of this lesson is about what "spread" means and what happens when it fails. The mechanism is two steps.
A hash function turns the key into a bucket index. The table stores the entry in that bucket. Search recomputes the same index and looks only there. If the buckets hold roughly one entry each, that lookup touches one entry and the cost is constant.
If every key lands in bucket 0, the lookup walks a list of n entries and the cost is O of n — the same as the unsorted array, with extra arithmetic on top.
Slide 5 names the three properties a hash function must have: deterministic (the same key always gives the same index), uniform (keys spread evenly over the buckets), and fast to compute, using the whole key. Deterministic is not a nice-to-have.
If h("Ada") returns 3 on insert and 5 on search, the entry is unreachable and the map is broken, not slow. Slide 5 also gives the division method, h(k) = k mod m, with the warning to choose m prime and not close to a power of 2. The reason is uniformity.
With m = 16, k mod 16 keeps only the low 4 bits of k, so any set of keys that agrees in those bits — student IDs ending in 00, timestamps on a 16 ms tick — piles into one bucket. A prime m mixes all the bits of k into the index instead.
The last quantity is the load factor alpha = n / m, where n is the number of entries and m is the number of buckets. Slide 13 uses it to split the two collision strategies: separate chaining keeps entries in lists outside the array and lets alpha exceed 1, while open addressing keeps everything inside the array and must stay below 1.
Both give O of 1 average and O of n worst case — slide 13 states both columns explicitly.
One hash function, three outcomes. The O of 1 average lives on the middle branch; the O of n worst case lives on the bottom one.
A hash table is a cloakroom with m numbered hooks. The hash function is the rule the attendant uses to decide which hook your coat goes on: h(k) = k mod m. Hand over a coat and the attendant computes the hook, hangs the coat, and writes nothing down.
Come back with the same ticket and the attendant recomputes the same hook and finds your coat immediately — that is the O of 1 average. When two coats hash to the same hook, the attendant hangs the second coat on the same hook (chaining, slide 9: 50, 85 and 92 all hang on hook 1) or walks along the rail to the next free hook (open addressing, slide 11: 49 wants hook 9, finds it taken, takes hook 0).
Either way you now have to look at more than one coat. If every coat hashes to hook 1, the attendant stands at hook 1 and lifts coats one at a time until yours appears. That is O of n, and no amount of arithmetic changes it.
The cloakroom has a physical rail, so a full hook is obvious and the attendant can see the whole row at a glance. A hash table has no such view: open addressing can only follow the probe sequence one slot at a time, which is why deleting an entry needs a tombstone (slide 13) rather than simply removing the coat — pulling a coat off the rail would break the chain of slots that later searches must walk through.
Chaining, m = 7, new entries go to the end of the chain (slide 9's convention). Every key landed in its own bucket, so alpha = 5/7 about 0.71 and every search costs one comparison. Now add 64 and 36, both of which collide: search(18): compute 18 mod 7 = 4, look at bucket 4, compare 18 with 18, return the value.
1 comparison. search(36): compute 36 mod 7 = 1, look at bucket 1, compare 36 with 57 (no), compare 36 with 64 (no), compare 36 with 36 (yes). 3 comparisons. search(50): compute 50 mod 7 = 1, walk the whole chain 57, 64, 36 and find nothing.
3 comparisons and a failed search — the worst case for a lookup is a miss, because you must exhaust the chain to be sure. With n = 7 and m = 7, alpha = 1.0. The average chain length is 1, but the longest chain is 3, and that is the number the exam will ask you to count.
Trace a linear-probing insertion the way you will on paper, with slide 11's example: insert 89, 18, 49, 58, 69 into m = 10 with h(k) = k mod 10. Probe h(k), then h(k)+1, h(k)+2, wrapping past 9 back to 0, and count every slot you examine, the first one included. Write the empty table and the rule. Draw slots 0 to 9.
Write the rule at the top: h(k) = k mod 10, probe forward, wrap at 9 back to 0. Every probe is one slot examined, including the first. Insert 89 and 18. 89 mod 10 = 9: slot 9 is empty, so place 89 there. 18 mod 10 = 8: slot 8 is empty, so place 18 there. 1 probe each. Insert 49: the first collision. 49 mod 10 = 9.
Slot 9 holds 89, so probe on: wrap to slot 0, which is empty. Place 49 at slot 0. 2 probes (slots 9, 0). Insert 58: walk the run. 58 mod 10 = 8. Slots 8 (18), 9 (89) and 0 (49) are taken, so the next try is slot 1, which is empty. Place 58 at slot 1. 4 probes (slots 8, 9, 0, 1). Insert 69: the run grows again.
69 mod 10 = 9. Slots 9 (89), 0 (49) and 1 (58) are taken, so try slot 2: empty. Place 69 at slot 2. 4 probes (slots 9, 0, 1, 2). Write the final table. Final table: 0 to 49, 1 to 58, 2 to 69, 3 to 7 empty, 8 to 18, 9 to 89, exactly as on slide 11. Probes per insert: 1, 1, 2, 4, 4. Load factor alpha = 5/10 = 0.5.
A hash table search is O of 1, so it is always at least as fast as a balanced BST. Slide 13 lists the worst case for both chaining and open addressing as O of n, and the average only holds when the hash function is uniform and alpha is kept in check.
If every key hashes to the same bucket, search walks all n entries — strictly worse than a balanced BST's guaranteed O of log n, because you also paid the hash computation.
The balanced BST's O of log n is a worst-case bound; the hash table's O of 1 is an average that depends on a property of your hash function, not on the data structure alone. On an exam, "O of 1" written without "average" for a hash table is a lost mark.
Last year's paper asks you to state the number of probes needed to insert a key into a linear-probing table. Before you move on, write down the one sentence you would give a classmate who counts only the collisions and forgets to count the first probe.
Then check it against the probe counts you wrote in the walkthrough.
